newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer says knows of no changes to Buba laws.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says knows of no changes to Buba laws.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday he was not aware of any plans to cut the size of the German central bank's council after the start of European monetary union.
"As far as I have been informed, there are no plans to change the Bundesbank laws in such a way," Tietmeyer told a news conference after a fortnightly council meeting.

Germany's Bild newspaper reported on Thursday that the Bonn government has plans to change the Bundesbank law to reduce the number of council members and employees, cut the length of terms served and also reduce pay.

Friedrich Merz, a financial expert for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told Bild that after the scheduled introduction of the new euro in 1999 there would be no need for such a large number of Bundesbank officials.

"If monetary union comes in 1999, we won't need a 17-member central bank council and 16,000 Bundesbank employees any more," Merz told the newspaper. "New council members should therefore no longer be appointed for eight-year terms."

Another CDU member, Heinz Schemken told Bild: "If the Bundesbank law is changed ... salaries should be cut. It is not right that the Bundesbank president should earn more than the Chancellor and that Bundesbank council members should earn more than government ministers in Bonn."

The Bundesbank, which has 17 council members including eight directorate members, itself said in April that it planned to streamline its branch network, cutting down the number of branches to a target of 128 from 167 at the end of 1996.
Members of the central bank's directorate are nominated by the federal cabinet and, after consultation, appointed for a period of normally eight, but certainly not less than two years.
